props.kicker: POSTSCRIPT · HOW THE U.S. CONSUMER WAS BUILT
props.title: August 1945: the war ends
props.note: Housel postscript. Book-dated history, not a forecast.

rows.v: 16 million Americans — 11% of the population — served. About 8 million were overseas. Average age 23.
Within 18 months all but 1.5 million were home and out of uniform.
Fewer than 12,000 homes a month built in 1943 — less than one new home per American city.
1946 Council of Economic Advisors to Truman: risk of a full-scale depression in the next one to four years.
Ships, tanks, and planes stopped almost overnight. Marriage spiked. Soldiers wanted a home and a job immediately.

props.title: Spending became policy
props.note: Fed not independent until 1951, as the book states.

rows.v: In 1942 the Fed said it would keep short-term rates at 0.38% to finance the war. They did not budge for seven years.
Three-month Treasury yields stayed below 2% until the mid-1950s.
The explicit aim: keep the cost of financing the equivalent of $6 trillion of war spending low.
16 million veterans: often no money down, no interest in year one, payments that could beat rent.
First credit card 1950. Interest on debt, including cards, was tax deductible then. Household debt in the 1950s grew 1.5× faster than in the 2000s splurge.

props.title: Debt, homes, and a new normal

rows.v: Household debt-to-income just over 100% when Housel wrote. Through the 1950s–1970s it stayed below 60%.
Homeownership 47% in 1900, about there for four decades, 53% by 1945, 62% by 1970.
Real income for the bottom 20% grew by a nearly identical amount as the top 5% from 1950 to 1980.
Today's consumer expectations were trained in a unique postwar machine — cheap credit, houses, and a culture that told people to spend.
Your grandparents' 'everyone had a house and a pension' is a specific era, not a human constant. Chapter 1 again.
Commercial car and truck making nearly ceased 1942–1945. Then 21 million cars sold 1945–1949, another 37 million by 1955.
Just under 2 million homes built 1940–1945. Then 7 million from 1945–1950, another 8 million by 1955.
Fed to Truman, 1951: consumer spending plus residential construction about $203 billion — around 40% above 1944.
Average wages doubled 1940–1948, then doubled again by 1963. The country got rich by making the poor less poor.
Share of national income after tax for the roughly $16,000-and-over group: from 13% to 7% by 1945, as cited.
Women's labor force participation: 31% after the war, 37% by 1955, 40% by 1965.
Normal people drove Chevys, rich people Cadillacs — similar engines. Three TV stations put tens of millions in sync each night.
Household debt increased fivefold 1947–1957, but incomes rose fast and starting debt was low, so the ratio stayed manageable — still below 60% even after the 1970s.
Recession: unemployment highest since the 1930s. Inflation stayed high. Short-term rates 8% in 1973, up from 2.5% a decade earlier.
The crack: winds turned uneven, but expectations stayed in a 1945–1980 equality-of-lifestyle world. That gap still trains how people spend.

props.title: Expectations outlived the era that trained them
props.note: Postscript close. Book-dated history, not a forecast.

rows.v: Cheap credit, a housing boom, and a culture of spend built a specific American consumer after 1945.
From about 1950 to 1980, the bottom and the top could feel they were in the same lifestyle movie.
Winds turned uneven. Incomes and luck diverged. The 1945–1980 script did not update as fast.
Your grandparents' 'normal' was a postwar policy accident, not a law of money. That is why no one is crazy.
Do not copy a 1955 household as if it were a template. Copy the behaviour: enough, slack, and time.
